Paint one illustration of a single moment from Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland.

RULES (they outrank everything below):
1) No text or symbols anywhere: no letters, numbers, signage, logos or inscriptions, no writing on labels, bottles, books, signs, slates or playing cards, and no artist's signature or initials in a corner.
2) One scene painted to every edge of the frame: no panels, collage, border, frame, margin, visible paper or blank backdrop, and never a photographed painting or mockup.
3) Nothing from outside the moment's era.
4) Natural anatomy: no extra or malformed limbs, hands or faces.
5) sexually explicit content and lingering gore are never shown; serious depictions of battles, blood and death and non-sexual nudity may be, treated seriously.
6) No likeness of any real actor, performer or public figure.
7) A character you draw from CANON keeps exactly that look. Anyone else the moment needs appears as an unnamed figure with an ordinary, different face.

MOMENT (A Mad Tea-Party ¶13 to A Mad Tea-Party ¶20): "“Do you mean that you think you can find out the answer to it?” said the March Hare. “Exactly so,” said Alice. “Then you should say what you mean,” the March Hare went on. “I do,” Alice hastily replied; “at least—at least I mean what I say—that’s the same thing, you know.” “Not the same thing a bit!” said the Hatter. “You might just as well say that ‘I see what I eat’ is the same thing as ‘I eat what I see’!” “You might just as well say,” added the March Hare, “that ‘I like what I get’ is the same thing as ‘I get what I like’!” “You might just as well say,” added the Dormouse, who seemed to be talking in his sleep, “that ‘I breathe when I sleep’ is the same thing as ‘I sleep when I breathe’!” “It _is_ the same thing with you,” said the Hatter, and here the conversation dropped, and the party sat silent for a minute, while Alice thought over all she could remember about ravens and writing-desks, which wasn’t much."

CONTEXT (for understanding only; paint the moment above):
- Before: “Come, we shall have some fun now!” thought Alice. “I’m glad they’ve begun asking riddles.—I believe I can guess that,” she added aloud.

When someone speaks, show the speaker and listeners where they are; never paint the content of the speech as a separate scene or as figures beside them. Figures of speech and comparisons are not literal objects. Infer time, light, weather and any place not given under SETTING from the text and context.

WORK BRIEF (alice-in-wonderland; what may be shown; it outranks the style):
Tone: Whimsical and dreamlike, with a gently unsettling bewilderment that turns to sharp absurdity at court.
Depiction: Alice's changing size reads clearly against doors, furniture, trees and other figures.
Depiction: Talking animals are drawn as animals, with human posture and dress where the text gives it.
Depiction: Playing-card courtiers, gardeners and soldiers are flat, oblong cards with heads, arms and legs.
Depiction: Threats and executions stay threats or slapstick; no gore or real injury.
Depiction: Take no likeness, costume or prop from film or animated adaptations.
Era: Victorian England and its dream Wonderland
People: Alice, a young Victorian English girl, among talking animals, card courtiers and odd Wonderland folk.
Dress: A Victorian child's dress and pinafore for Alice; period robes, waistcoats and hats for others.
Buildings and objects: Riverbank, rabbit-hole, long hall, little door, cottages, mushroom wood, croquet-ground and courtroom.
Technology: Pocket watches, oil lamps, slates and pencils; no machines or modern devices.

SETTING (where this passage happens; set the moment here and keep the place's fixed features, unless the moment is plainly somewhere else):
- Tea-table under a tree: a large wooden table set out in the open under a spreading tree, in front of a house, with a cloth laid across it and many tea-things and cups scattered over its surface. The tree shades the table, with leafy branches and a rough trunk. The house stands behind it with a plain, old-fashioned Victorian front. Ground is level grass before the table.

CANON, NAMED HERE (fixed look; the moment decides pose, expression, clothing changes and action):
- March Hare: an anthropomorphic hare standing upright with human posture and dress, long upright ears, brown-and-tawny fur, adult in age, lean and slightly hunched build, a long muzzle with whiskers, round wide-set eyes, a wild restless look. He wears a rumpled period waistcoat, shirt and tailcoat in muted brown and cream, with a loose cravat and a tall hat tilted askew. He carries a teacup or teapot as his signature prop.
- Hatter: an adult Victorian man of middle years, lean and slightly stooped, with untidy hair in need of cutting and a long pale face. He wears a shabby period waistcoat and frock coat with a tall, battered hat that is sometimes not his own. Colours are faded browns and greys with a dingy cravat. He carries a teacup and a slice of bread-and-butter, and an old pocket watch.
- Alice: a young Victorian English girl of about seven, slight and small-boned, who grows very tall and shrinks very small over the course of her adventures. Skin fair with a light sunburn; long straight light-brown hair that often falls loose into her eyes, which she tosses back with a little shake of her head; bright, eager, curious features. Signature outfit: a pale yellow Victorian child's frock with short puffed sleeves and a sky-blue sash, a white pinafore with frilled shoulder straps, blue-and-white striped stockings and black strap shoes. Carries no props of her own.
- the Dormouse: a small, drowsy talking dormouse, grey-brown fur with a pale belly, round ears, a thin tail and small whiskers, standing and sitting upright in human posture. Age: adult. Build: slight and plump. Skin: grey-brown fur. Face: small dark eyes that are often shut, a pink nose, long whiskers. Signature outfit: a faded blue waistcoat with a small brass button and a dull green neckcloth. Signature prop: a china teacup held in its small paws.

Rendering: Stylized, painterly, mysterious and expansive. The painterly treatment belongs to the depicted world itself, not to a photographed physical artwork.
Palette: Mature, grounded color; rich but restrained contrast.
Lighting: Luminous, dramatic lighting.
Materials and texture: Gritty, raw texture; avoid polished digital smoothness.
Composition: Cinematic, immersive viewpoint; heroic but grounded.
Negatives: Avoid photorealism or a photographic look. Avoid childish/cartoonish styling. Never present the scene as a painting on a wall, gallery piece, framed artwork, fresco, mural, poster, manuscript page, or printed illustration. Do not show canvas texture, paper edges, matting, border, mockup, or surrounding room. The depicted world must fill the image edge-to-edge.

FRAME: one continuous scene painted to every edge, 16:9 widescreen landscape.
